t: #3371 Identify the Largest Outlier in an Array
o: Exactly n−2 elements are 'special'; one of the other two equals their sum, and the last one is the outlier. We want the largest value that can serve as the outlier. Let T be the total sum. If x is the outlier and y is the sum element, then T = x + y + y, so y = (T − x)/2. Thus x is a valid outlier iff T − x is even and y exists elsewhere in the array (at a distinct index). Example 1: T = 20; x = 10 gives y = 5, present → answer 10. Example 3 shows duplicates matter: with five 1s, sum 5 and outlier 5 coexist.
k: Key identity: T = outlier + 2 × (sum element), so the sum element is determined by the outlier: y = (T − x)/2.
A frequency map lets us verify y exists at a different index by temporarily decrementing count of x.
Enumerate every element as a candidate outlier and take the maximum valid one.

a.i: For each element x treated as the outlier, the required sum element is forced to be (T − x)/2. Check parity, look it up in a frequency map (excluding x's own occurrence), and keep the largest valid x.
s: Compute total sum T and a frequency map of all values.
For each x in nums: if (T − x) is odd, skip.
Temporarily decrement count[x]; if count[(T − x)/2] > 0, x is a valid outlier.
Restore count[x] and record the maximum valid x.
a.t: O(n) — one pass to build counts and sum, one pass to test each candidate.
a.sp: O(n) for the frequency map (values bounded by ±1000, so effectively O(1)).

a.i: Same math, but verify existence of y with sorting and binary search instead of a hash map — useful when memory for a map is undesirable.
s: Sort a copy of nums and compute T.
For each x, skip if T − x is odd; otherwise binary search for y = (T − x)/2.
Ensure the found index corresponds to a different occurrence than x (check a neighbor if indices collide).
a.t: O(n log n) — sorting dominates; each of n candidates does one binary search.
a.sp: O(n) for the sorted copy (or O(1) extra if sorting in place is acceptable).

w: Prefer the hash-map approach: linear time and trivially correct. The main pitfall is duplicate handling — when x equals y, you must ensure they come from different indices, hence the temporary decrement. Another pitfall is skipping negative outliers; values may be negative, so initialize the answer to −∞. A follow-up might ask for the smallest outlier or for counting all valid outliers.
